description.narrative:
1. PROTECT THE PUBLICS RESOURCES To build more prosperous societies, our public resources need to be protected and mobilized for the common good. Outcome 1.1: Maximum openness, transparency and responsiveness in public contracting Outcome 1.2: More effective prevention and exposure of public sector bribery, theft and abuse of power
2. STOP FLOWS OF DIRTY MONEY TI will work to close down domestic and international loopholes that allow perpetrators of corruption to hide, launder and enjoy their illegal proceeds. Outcome 2.1: Disabled systems for secret payments and concealment of assets Outcome 2.2: Increased accountability for corruptionenabling networks and gatekeepers
3. SECURE INTEGRITY IN POLITICS TI will promote the integrity of elections and inclusive access to power as well as foster new approaches where all stakeholders can exert equal influence in an open and transparent way. Outcome 3.1: Removal of undue influence from elections and political appointments Beredning av insats Appraisal of Intervention Contribution ID: 14089 11 (30) Outcome 3.2: Greater transparency, accountability and equity in influence over public decisionmaking
4. DRIVE INTEGRITY IN BUSINESS TI will look to elevate the norms of responsible business conduct with likeminded allies committed to anticorruption, as well as expost the lack of responsibility and integrity amongst powerful business interests that control political levers and resist change. Outcome 4.1: A critical mass of business leadership fulfilling strong integrity commitments Outcome 4.2: More effective exposure and punishment of corrupt business
5. PURSUE ENFORCEMENT AND JUSTICE To promote the independence and capacity of oversight and enforcement institutions, TI will look to activate its networks and partnerships to trigger action among enforcement authoritiess and put an end to impunity and check new power concentrations. Outcome 5.1: Strengthened independence, capacity and will to act for integrity institutions Outcome 5.2: Greater equity, consistency and removal of bias in corruption prosecutions and judicial outcomes Outcome 5.3: An effective international anticorruption enforcement framework
6. EXPAND CIVIC SPACE FOR ACCOUNTABILITY Corruption thrives when it faces no opposition from those who are affected by it. TI will look to work with multisectoral partners to ensure that activitivists, journalists and ordinary citizens are enabled and empowered o take action against corruption. Beredning av insats Appraisal of Intervention Contribution ID: 14089 12 (30) Outcome 6.1: Enhanced freedom and security for activists, whistleblowers and journalists to challenge abuse of power Outcome 6.2: Increased channels for people to demand results for the common good
7. BUILD COMMUNITY LEADERSHIP AGAINST CORRUPTION TI will work to nurture and support more leaders across government, business and civil society who understand and adopt values of integrity, accountability and responsible conduct as guiding principles for decision making. Outcome 7.1: Strengthened public discourse based on deeper understanding and acceptance of accountability values Outcome 7.2: A next generation of civic, public and business leaders better equipped to fight corruption
Through the new component Anti-corruption for strengthened SRHR, the following objectives are added for the year 2026:
Objective 1: Key Corruption Risks in SRHR Systems Diagnosed and Mapped
The project will produce a country-validated SRHR Integrity Diagnostic tool that identifies corruption risks using five core indicators, which are: Informal Payment Frequency, Essential Medicine Shortage Rates, Health Workforce Attendance for SRHR services, Denial of SRHR Services or Discriminatory Practices and Transparency and Accuracy of SRHR Budget.
Objective 2: Strengthening Accountability through Civic Engagement, Institutional Reform, and Capacity Enhancement
By the end of 2026, each TI Chapter will create a functional accountability pathway linking community reports to authorities, document institutional responses to verified cases, develop a harmonized accountability model for regional guidance, and implement a baseline measurement of government participation and responsiveness. Communities will have clearer pathways to raise SRHR integrity concerns, stronger skills to use evidence in advocacy, and documented examples of how their engagement has influenced change, focused on civic accountability Strengthening, Accountability Mechanism, Institutional Responsiveness, Collaboration Across Stakeholders.
Objective 3: Generate and Use Evidence to Influence Policy and Strengthen SRHR Governance
Expected results after 2026 is a first set of evidence-informed advocacy priorities agreed between communities, TI chapters, and authorities, providing a shared agenda for reducing SRHR-related corruption in the following years.
The key areas for assessing quality and impact of evidence in SRHR over a three year period will include: Quality of Evidence Base, Institutional Uptake of Evidence, Policy and Governmental Engagement, Early Signs of System-Level Change.
The above objectives are additional to the overarching objectives and expected results of the core support from the Unit Democracy and Human rights and specifically related to the Overarching objective 1 (SO1) as specified in TI's Strategic plan and below: Protect the Public Resources.

description.narrative:
Examples of results achieved Transparency International during operational year 2024:
All objectives (as mentioned above) are from TI's Strategy 2030: Holding Power to Account.
Strategic Objective 1 (SO1). PROTECT THE PUBLICS RESOURCES
Area: Integrating anticorruption into global development agendas * Result: Transparency International successfully advocated for corruption to be recognized as a crosscutting issue in the Elements Paper of the Fourth Financing for Development Agenda (FfD4). Their recommendations were included in the Elements paper that will shape the outcome document of the 2025 conference.This included stronger provisions to safeguard domestic public financial management systems, combat illicit financial flows, and protect debt negotiations and management from corruption. This will ultimately influence how countries and international financial institutions mobilise, prioritise, and invest resources for sustainable development. Background: When preparations for the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development began, anticorruption, transparency and accountability measures were notably absent.
* TI also contributed to the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights 2024 report at the Human Rights Council 56th session, which, building on TI's submission, acknowledged corruptions impact on public service delivery. Several of Transparency Internationals recommendations to close the loopholes for corruption in the service delivery cycle were included in the report.
Area: Exposing corruption in health care procurement (Zimbabwe) * Country example: TI published a Corruption Risk Assessment report on Zimbabwes health sector. The report focused on the countrys medical supply chain, revealing how essential medicines are diverted to the black market. Advocacy efforts by Transparency International Zimbabwe led the Medicines Control Agency to crack down on illegal sales and confiscate unregistered medicines, and the VicePresident of Zimbabwe to endorse an electronic procurement system to improve transparency in medical supply purchasing. Background: In parts of Africa, women and girls face multiple barriers when accessing education and health care, with corruption further limiting their access to these vital services. Through TI's All 4 Inclusive Service Delivery Africa project, they work to eliminate corruption that prevents them from exercising their rights in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ghana, Madagascar, Rwanda and Zimbabwe. TI also reflected that exposing corruption is just the first step by driving reform and holding those in power accountable, they are working toward a future where health care is not a privilege, but a right that no one is denied.
Area: Enhancing integrity in climate governance * TI also successfully lobbied the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change to remove a US$30,000 fee for local communities to appeal under the Paris Agreement.
Area: Expanding channels for reporting corruption * Legal services provided for free: For more than two decades, Transparency Internationals Advocacy and Legal Advice Centres (ALACs) have been a lifeline for individuals and communities seeking justice against corruption. Since 2003, ALACs have provided free support for over 350,000 individuals and investigated more than 85,000 corruption related cases. Their work goes far beyond resolving individual complaints it strengthens accountability systems, builds public trust, and empowers citizens to demand integrity from those in power. In 2024 alone, the ALACs supported over 10,000 clients in over 53 countries.
SO 2. STOP FLOWS OF DIRTY MONEY
Area: EU beneficial ownership transparency reform * Transparency International secured easier tracking of dirty money by ensuring that the EU requires member states to ensure broad access for civil society and the media to beneficial ownership registers, rather than casebycase access. Also, TI ensured that access by civil society and the media to these registers will not be restricted based on their nationality, and that provisions which exposed journalists and activists to risks of retaliation when accessing beneficial ownership registers were eliminated. Targeting enablers of corruption
* Transparency International leveraged evidence from their Loophole Masters report, published in December 2023, to shape global debates on the role of professionals from non-financial sectors (enablers) in facilitating illicit financial flows.
Area: Regional and national reforms *Transparency International engaged with the African Union on the need to develop regional beneficial ownership transparency standards.
Area: Anti-corruption advocacy with the G20 * Transparency International brought together civil society and G20 officials working on anticorruption for a lively discussion on the need for stronger G20 anticorruption measures. TI developed a narrative on sustainable development, inequality and financial integrity, and published a position paper targeting the G20. In addition, TI made a guerrilla marketing stunt in Rio de Janeiro which involved giant dollar bill paragliders in order to raise awareness of the G20s role in confronting corruption. They highlighted the critical role of anticorruption and financial integrity in promoting sustainable development and reducing inequality.
SO 3. SECURE INTEGRITY IN POLITICS
Area: Setting a high bar for political finance integrity * Transparency International adopted the Standards for Integrity in Political Finance, setting global principles comprising 55 recommendations for governments to ensure political funding is transparent to voters, originates from legitimate sources, ensures a level playing field, helps overcome financial hurdles facing women, preserves the neutrality of the state, and is subject to independent oversight. The Transparency International Standards leveraged evidence and extensive consultation across the movement, as well as from experts within governments, international organisations, election observers, civil society and think tanks from all continents. The standards inform their national Chapters gender-sensitive advocacy to improve political finance regulatory frameworks and practice, as well as their advocacy for these standards to inform the work of international election observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), the EU, Asia and the Pacific, the Americas and Africa, and of intergovernmental platforms such as the Open Government Partnership.
Area: Improving detection of political corruption risks in the Western Balkans and Türkiye * As part of the EU funded Citizen Engagement for Public Integrity project, Transparency International assessed governments capacity to fight corruption across the Western Balkans and Türkiye. The resulting National Integrity System reports identified how key institutions are performing and exposed their vulnerabilities, allowing chapters to advocate for the specific reforms needed in each country.
Area: Country specific anti-corruption efforts * Venezuela: Transparencia Venezuela documented and reported 314 violations of state neutrality ahead of the July presidential election and in its aftermath. The Chapter shared these reports with international observers, regional organisations overseeing human right violations, and the international community representatives in the country.
* United States: Transparency International US helped draft and ensure passage of the Foreign Extortion Prevention Act (2024), criminalizing bribes asked for or accepted by foreign officials from American entities. The US Department of Justice has already started receiving reports under this law. Hence, benefitting the fight against corruption in all developing countries (as well as in developed countries, of course).
SO 4. DRIVE INTEGRITY IN BUSINESS
Area: Promoting business integrity * Transparency International launched an integrity toolkit with the World Economic Forum to help medium-sized businesses implement ethical practices, the World Economic Forum (WEF) Business Integrity Toolkit. TI's work demonstrated the economic benefits of integrity, such as better market access, stronger partnerships and competitive advantage. The toolkit provides practical strategies and advice to help simplify this process, enabling businesses (even when they have limited resources) to operate more transparently and ethically, which ultimately protects peoples lives and livelihoods by reducing the harmful impact of corruption. For instance, the toolkit is now actively being used by businesses in Latin America and is being integrated into the supply chains of members of the WEF Partnership against Corruption Initiative (PACI).
SO 5. PURSUE ENFORCEMENT AND JUSTICE Pressing Britain to act in a Malawian corruption case * Transparency International advocated for action by the UK against Zuneth Sattar, accused of bribing senior Malawian officials in return for high-value public contracts, leading to commitments from the National Crime Agency to recover stolen Malawian funds, and increased media awareness of the case in Malawi.
Area: Investigating Bangladeshs corrupt former regime * Transparency International partnered with Bloomberg and The Observer to expose undeclared UK property investments by former Bangladeshi land minister Saifuzzaman Chowdhury, and we contributed to ongoing corruption investigations in Bangladesh and the UK.
Area: Pursuing Russian kleptocrats assets in France * Transparency International France filed legal complaints against the authorities for failing to act against Russian oligarchs hiding wealth in France. French authorities seized three properties, including one owned by the current husband of Putins ex-wife. TI also advocated for asset confiscation to compensate victims of corruption.
SO 6. EXPAND CIVIC SPACE FOR ACCOUNTABILITY
Area: Strengthening civic space through UNCAC * Transparency International organised the first ever civil society panel at the United Nations Convention against Corruption (UNCAC) to ensure that civic space features on the UNCAC agenda, and made recommendations on how UNCAC can contribute to an enabling environment for civil society. TI advocated for greater inclusion of civil society representatives in national delegations to UNCAC.
Area: Preventing repression in Bosnia and Herzegovina * TI led a successful campaign to block a law labelling foreign funded NGOs as foreign agents. TI's advocacy prompted the European Commission to warn Bosnia and Herzegovina not to reintroduce the law.
Area: Protecting civic space through the EU System for an Enabling Environment for civil society (EUSEE) * Transparency International built a network of national partners to monitor the enabling environment for civil society in 86 countries. This network developed a monitoring methodology for early warning of infringements against civic space, and comprehensive annual assessments. This was done as a part of the consortium implementing the EU System for an Enabling Environment for civil society (EUSEE) which is a new partnership between Transparency International, Hivos, CIVICUS, the European Partnership for Democracy, Focus and Democracy Reporting International. They built a network of national partners in 86 countries, which includes 15 of TI's national Chapters. Together, they developed a comprehensive monitoring methodology covering six principles and multiple dimensions of the enabling environment for civil society, and devised a linking and learning strategy to strengthen civil society capacities to protect and expand civic space. The EUSEE monitoring system began reporting in late 2024.
SO 7. BUILD COMMUNITY LEADERSHIP AGAINST CORRUPTION
Area: Empowering young people in the fight against corruption * TI saw increased participation in Transparency Internationals bootcamps and Transparency Schools in 2024, especially among young people. Across the Transparency International movement, TI supported youth leadership to tackle corruption, recognizing their role and potential to drive change.
Area: International Anti-Corruption Conference (IACC) in Vilnius in June 2024 * Transparency International hosted over 2,200 delegates from more than 140 countries and organised over 120 sessions on anticorruption solutions.
* The conference featured global anticorruption leaders, including heads of state, civil society leaders and investigative journalists.
* TI connected 1 693 people through an anticorruption app and involved more than 2,000 members of the public in the Fighting Corruption Music Festival. TI also hosted the eight Films for Transparency festival focusing on the power of film as an advocacy tool in the fight against corruption.
Area: Expanding youth activism and training *Transparency International brought together 10 Integrity Ambassadors in Zimbabwe to support health and education initiatives for vulnerable groups.
